Render as a 1940s Golden-Age comic-book illustration in the style of early *Superman* and
*Captain America* covers. Convert any provided photograph into hand-drawn cel-style art —
this should read as a printed vintage comic, not a modern digital illustration or a
photograph.

- **Linework:** Bold, confident black ink outlines with varied weight. Clean cel art —
  shapes are drawn and filled, not painted.
- **Color:** Large unbroken fields of solid FLAT color. Restricted four-color-press
  palette — roughly 5–7 ink colors total: red, blue, yellow, flesh tone, black, and cream.

  rendered gradients, and NO Ben-Day dot halftones (dots are the pop-art style, not this

  newsprint / cream tone in cover mode, or a single saturated color field per panel in
  story mode.

  working on. Everything else simplifies to flat color and bold outline.

  identifiable real people — simplified inked features, not photorealistic portraits.

  kids building something real.

- Render ONLY the text specified for the chosen composition — exact wording, nothing else.
- Do NOT invent any other posters, signs, slogans, labels, or lettering. All other
  background surfaces are blank.

  diagrams. Give them physically plausible front grippers, pushers, hooks, or arms. When

large fields — it belongs on edges, machinery, and shadow.

The engineer, carrying a briefcase and notebook on his way into work, has stopped on the sidewalk — surprised and amused, not frightened. The joke: the visitors have mistaken an ordinary engineer for someone who can take them to the leader of Earth's technological civilization. Low heroic angle, strong diagonals, the saucer dominating center, the three figures in a strong triangular arrangement.
iterations.prompt:
A 1940s Golden Age American comic-book cover illustration, in the tradition of early Superman and Captain America covers: bold hand-inked black outlines, large unbroken areas of flat color, dramatic heroic composition, and a classic four-color printing aesthetic. This is authentic 1940s comic-book production art — hand-drawn and inked, wide 4×6 landscape (3:2). NOT photorealism, NOT painterly, NOT a modern flat-vector poster.

RENDERING: Use a restricted Golden Age palette of about 5–7 vivid ink colors — League orange (#F47920), primary blue, bright yellow, red, flesh tones, black, and white. Shadows are bold FLAT BLACK shapes with hard edges; no soft gradients, no airbrush, no cross-hatching, no Ben-Day or halftone dots, and no surface grain, speckle, or aged-paper texture anywhere. Colors stay bright and clean, like freshly printed comic art.

Spend rich, confident inked detail ONLY on: the child, the humanoid robot, the flying saucer, and the engineer. Simplify everything else — building, trees, plaza — into bold graphic shapes with minimal architectural detail.

THE SCENE: The landscaped central lawn of a sleek modern corporate research campus. A simplified glass-and-concrete engineering building fills the background, with the word "QUALCOMM" spelled exactly Q-U-A-L-C-O-M-M in clean blue sans-serif letters mounted on the side of the building. A broad grassy plaza with sidewalks, a few trees and flowering shrubs. At the center-left of the lawn a classic 1950s flying saucer has just landed: a polished silver disc with a domed top, simple rivets, and a glowing landing ring, rendered in flat comic-book color rather than reflective realism, its ramp lowered. Two visitors have stepped out: (1) a confident young inventor, about 13, in jeans and a red t-shirt with tousled hair, standing with one hand extended toward the engineer in greeting; and (2) beside the kid, a friendly HUMANOID ROBOT standing in a proud, HEROIC pose with both HANDS ON ITS HIPS, elbows out, chest up, chin high — an optimistic Golden Age vision of robotics, upright, mechanical, expressive and obviously friendly. Facing them on the sidewalk at the right is an ENGINEER — clearly a working tech engineer, NOT a businessman: an untucked collared shirt or polo with the sleeves pushed up, an ID badge on a lanyard around his neck, glasses, a laptop tucked under one arm. He has just arrived for work and stopped short — surprised and amused, not frightened. Compose from a low heroic angle with strong diagonals and bold silhouettes; the saucer anchors the composition and the child, robot, and engineer form a strong triangular arrangement that tells the story instantly.

The joke: the visitors have mistaken an ordinary engineer for someone who can take them to the leader of Earth's technological civilization.

TEXT — render ONLY these two pieces of lettering, nothing else: (1) EXACTLY ONE hand-lettered comic speech balloon, spoken by the child, reading exactly: "Take us to your leader." and (2) the word "QUALCOMM" (spelled Q-U-A-L-C-O-M-M) on the side of the building. No other speech balloon, caption, narration box, poster, sign, logo, label, or text anywhere.
